8.1: This reflection also helps to remove the desire for empty fame: that it is no longer in your power to have lived the whole of your life, or at least your life from your youth onwards, like a philosopher; but both to many others and to yourself it is plain that you are far from philosophy. You have fallen into disorder, then, so that it is no longer easy for you to get the reputation of a philosopher; and your way of life also stands against it. If, then, you have truly seen where the matter lies, throw away the thought of how you will seem to others, and be content if you live the rest of your life in the way your nature wills. Observe, then, what it wills, and let nothing else distract you; for you have had experience of many wanderings without having found happiness anywhere—not in syllogisms, nor in wealth, nor in reputation, nor in enjoyment, nor anywhere. Where is it, then? In doing what man's nature requires. How, then, shall a man do this? If he has principles from which his impulses and his acts come. What principles? Those which relate to good and bad: the belief that there is nothing good for a man which does not make him just, self-controlled, manly, free; and that there is nothing bad which does not do the opposite of what has been mentioned.
8.2: On the occasion of every act ask yourself: How does this stand with me? Shall I regret it? A little time and I am dead, and all is gone. What more do I seek, if what I am now doing is the work of an intelligent living being, and a social being, and one who is under the same law as God?
8.3: Alexander and Caius and Pompeius, what are they in comparison with Diogenes and Heraclitus and Socrates? For these men knew things, and their causes, or forms, and their matter, and the ruling principles of these men were the same, or in keeping with their pursuits. But as for the others, how many things they had to care for, and to how many things they were slaves!
8.4: Consider that men will do the same things all the same, even if you should burst.
8.5: This is the chief thing: do not be disturbed, for all things are according to the nature of the universe; and in a little while you will be nobody and nowhere, like Hadrianus and Augustus. Next, having fixed your eyes steadily on your business, look at it, and at the same time, remembering that it is your duty to be a good man, and what man's nature demands, do that without turning aside; and speak as seems to you most just, only let it be with a good disposition, with modesty, and without hypocrisy.
8.6: The nature of the universe has this work to do—to move to that place the things which are in this one, to change them, to take them away from here, and to carry them there. All things are change, yet we need not fear anything new. All things are familiar to us; and the distribution of them still remains the same.
8.7: Every nature is content with itself when it goes on its way well; and a rational nature goes on its way well when in its thoughts it assents to nothing false or uncertain, when it directs its impulses to social acts only, when it limits its desires and aversions to the things which are in its power, and when it is satisfied with everything that is assigned to it by the common nature. For every particular nature is a part of this common nature, as the nature of the leaf is a part of the nature of the plant; except that in the plant the nature of the leaf is part of a nature which has neither perception nor reason, and can be impeded; but the nature of man is part of a nature which cannot be impeded, and is intelligent and just, since it gives to everything in equal portions and according to its worth: times, substance, cause or form, activity, and circumstance. But examine things, not to discover that any one thing compared with any other single thing is equal in all respects, but by taking all the parts of one thing together and comparing them with all the parts of another together.
8.8: You do not have the leisure or the ability to read. But you have the leisure, or the ability, to check arrogance: you have the leisure to rise above pleasure and pain: you have the leisure to rise above the love of fame, and not to be irritated at stupid and ungrateful people—indeed, even to care for them.
8.9: Let no one hear you any longer finding fault with life at court, or with your own.
8.10: Regret is a kind of self-reproach for having neglected something useful; but what is good must be something useful, and the perfectly good man should look after it. But no such man would ever regret having refused any sensual pleasure. Pleasure, then, is neither good nor useful.
8.11: This thing, what is it in itself, in its own makeup? What is its substance and material? And what is its causal nature, or form? And what is it doing in the world? And how long does it last?
8.12: When you get up from sleep reluctantly, remember that it is in keeping with your constitution and with human nature to perform social acts, but sleeping is something we share even with irrational animals. And what is according to each individual's nature is also more particularly its own, and more suited to its nature, and indeed also more pleasant.
8.13: Constantly, and, if possible, on the occasion of every impression on the soul, apply to it the principles of Physics, of Ethics, and of Dialectic.
8.14: Whatever man you meet, immediately say to yourself: What opinions does this man have about good and bad? For if he has such and such opinions about pleasure and pain and the causes of each, and about fame and disgrace, death and life, it will seem nothing remarkable or strange to me if he does such and such things; and I shall bear in mind that he is compelled to do so.
8.15: Remember that just as it is a shame to be surprised if the fig tree produces figs, so it is to be surprised if the world produces such and such things as it is in its nature to produce; and for the physician and the helmsman it is a shame to be surprised if a man has a fever, or if the wind is against them.
8.16: Remember that to change your opinion and to follow someone who corrects your error is as consistent with freedom as it is to persist in your error. For it is your own—the activity which is carried out according to your own impulse and judgement, and indeed according to your own understanding too.
8.17: If a thing is in your own power, why do you do it? But if it is in the power of another, whom do you blame—the atoms, that is, chance, or the gods? Both are foolish. You must blame nobody. For if you can, correct the cause; but if you cannot do this, at least correct the thing itself; but if you cannot do even this, what use is it to you to find fault? For nothing should be done without a purpose.
8.18: What has died does not fall out of the universe. If it stays here, it also changes here, and is dissolved into its proper parts, which are elements of the universe and of yourself. And these too change, and they do not grumble.
8.19: Everything exists for some end—a horse, a vine. Why are you surprised? Even the sun will say, I am for some purpose, and the rest of the gods will say the same. For what purpose, then, are you here—to enjoy pleasure? See if common sense allows this.
8.20: Nature has had regard in everything no less to the end than to the beginning and the continuation, just like the man who throws up a ball. What good is it, then, to the ball to be thrown up, or what harm for it to come down, or even to have fallen? And what good is it to the bubble while it holds together, or what harm when it has burst? The same may be said of a lamp too.
8.21:
Turn the body inside out, and see what kind of thing it is; and what kind of thing it becomes when it has grown old, and when it is diseased.

Short-lived are both the praiser and the praised, the one who remembers and the one remembered: and all this in a corner of this part of the world; and not even here do all agree, no, not even anyone with himself: and the whole earth too is a point.
8.22:
Attend to the matter in front of you, whether it is an opinion or an act or a word.

You suffer this justly: for you would rather become good tomorrow than be good today.
8.23: Am I doing anything? I do it with reference to the good of mankind. Does anything happen to me? I accept it and refer it to the gods, and to the source of all things, from which all that happens is derived.
8.24: Just as bathing appears to you—oil, sweat, dirt, filthy water, all disgusting things—so is every part of life and everything.
8.25: Lucilla saw Verus die, and then Lucilla died. Secunda saw Maximus die, and then Secunda died. Epitynchanus saw Diotimus die, and then Epitynchanus died. Antoninus saw Faustina die, and then Antoninus died. Such is everything. Celer saw Hadrianus die, and then Celer died. And those sharp-witted men, either seers or men puffed up with pride, where are they—for instance the sharp-witted men Charax and Demetrius the Platonist, and Eudaemon, and anyone else like them? All short-lived, dead long ago. Some indeed have not been remembered even for a short time, and others have become the heroes of fables, and others again have disappeared even from fables. Remember this, then: that this little compound, yourself, must either be dissolved, or your poor breath must be put out, or be moved and placed elsewhere.
8.26: It is satisfaction to a man to do the proper work of a man. Now it is a proper work of a man to be kind to his own kind, to despise the movements of the senses, to form a just judgement of plausible appearances, and to survey the nature of the universe and the things which happen in it.
8.27: There are three relations between you and other things: the first to the body which surrounds you; the second to the divine cause from which all things come to all; and the third to those who live with you.
8.28: Pain is either an evil to the body—then let the body say what it thinks of it—or to the soul; but it is in the power of the soul to keep its own serenity and tranquillity, and not to think that pain is an evil. For every judgement and impulse and desire and aversion is within, and no evil climbs so high.
8.29: Wipe out your imaginings by often saying to yourself: Now it is in my power to let no badness be in this soul, nor desire, nor any disturbance at all; but looking at all things I see what their nature is, and I use each according to its value.—Remember this power which you have from nature.
8.30: Speak both in the senate and to every man, whoever he may be, appropriately, without any affectation: use plain speech.
8.31: Augustus' court, wife, daughter, descendants, ancestors, sister, Agrippa, kinsmen, intimates, friends; Areius, Maecenas, physicians, and sacrificing priests—the whole court is dead. Then turn to the rest, considering not the death of a single man but of a whole family, as of the Pompeii; and what is inscribed on the tombs—The last of his line. Then consider what trouble those before them took so that they might leave a successor; and then, that of necessity someone must be the last. Again, here consider the death of a whole family.
8.32: It is your duty to order your life well in every single act; and if every act does its duty as far as possible, be content; and no one is able to stop you so that each act does not do its duty.—But something external will stand in the way. Nothing will stand in the way of your acting justly and soberly and thoughtfully.—But perhaps some other active power will be hindered. Well, by accepting the hindrance and by being content to transfer your efforts to what is allowed, another opportunity for action is immediately put before you in place of the one that was hindered, and one which will fit in with this ordering we are speaking of.
8.33: Receive wealth or prosperity without arrogance; and be ready to let it go.
8.34: If you have ever seen a hand cut off, or a foot, or a head, lying anywhere apart from the rest of the body, that is what a man makes of himself, as far as he can, when he is not content with what happens, and separates himself from others, or does anything unsociable. Suppose that you have detached yourself from the natural unity—for you were made by nature a part, but now you have cut yourself off—yet here there is this beautiful provision, that it is in your power to unite yourself again. God has allowed this to no other part, once it has been separated and cut apart, to come together again. But consider the kindness by which he has distinguished man, for he has put it in his power not to be separated at all from the universal; and when he has been separated, he has allowed him to return and to be united and to take up his place as a part again.
8.35: Just as the nature of the universe has given to every rational being all the other powers that it has, so we have received from it this power also. For as the universal nature turns to its use and fixes in its destined place everything which stands in the way and opposes it, and makes such things a part of itself, so also the rational being is able to make every hindrance its own material, and to use it for whatever purposes it may have intended.
8.36: Do not disturb yourself by thinking of the whole of your life. Do not let your thoughts take in all at once the various troubles which you may expect to come upon you: but on every occasion ask yourself, What is there in this which is unbearable and past enduring? For you will be ashamed to admit it. Next, remember that neither the future nor the past pains you, but only the present. And this is reduced to a very little, if only you set limits to it, and scold your mind if it is unable to hold out against even this.
8.37: Do Panthea or Fergamus now sit by the tomb of Verus? Do Chaurias or Diotimus sit by the tomb of Hadrianus? That would be ridiculous. Well, suppose they did sit there, would the dead be aware of it? And if the dead were aware, would they be pleased? And if they were pleased, would that make them immortal? Was it not in the order of destiny that these people too should first become old women and old men and then die? What, then, would those others do after these were dead? All this is foul smell and blood in a bag.
8.38: If you can see sharply, look and judge wisely, says the philosopher.
8.39: In the constitution of the rational being I see no virtue which is opposed to justice; but I see a virtue which is opposed to love of pleasure, and that is self-control.
8.40: If you take away your opinion about what seems to give you pain, you yourself stand in perfect security.—Who is this self?—Reason.—But I am not reason.—So be it. Then let the reason itself not trouble itself. But if any other part of you suffers, let it have its own opinion about itself.
8.41: Hindrance to the perceptions of the senses is an evil to the animal nature. Hindrance to the impulses, or desires, is equally an evil to the animal nature. And something else is equally an obstacle and an evil to the constitution of plants. So, then, what is a hindrance to the intelligence is an evil to the intelligent nature. Apply all these things, then, to yourself. Does pain or sensual pleasure affect you? The senses will see to that. Has any obstacle opposed you in your efforts towards an object? If indeed you were making this effort absolutely, without any reservation, certainly this obstacle is an evil to you considered as a rational being. But if you take into account the usual course of things, you have not yet been harmed nor even impeded. The things, however, which belong to the understanding no other man is in the habit of impeding, for neither fire, nor iron, nor tyrant, nor abuse touches it in any way. When it has been made a sphere, it stays a sphere.
8.42: It is not right that I should give myself pain, for I have never intentionally given pain even to another.
8.43: Different things delight different people; but my delight is to keep the ruling faculty sound, without turning away either from any man or from any of the things which happen to men, but looking at and receiving all with welcoming eyes, and using everything according to its value.
8.44: See that you secure this present time for yourself: for those who would rather pursue fame after death do not consider that the men of later times will be exactly like these whom they cannot bear now; and both are mortal. And what is it in any way to you if these men of later times make this or that sound, or have this or that opinion about you?
8.45: Take me and throw me where you will; for there I shall keep my divine part tranquil, that is, content, if it can feel and act in keeping with its proper constitution. Is this change of place a sufficient reason why my soul should be unhappy and worse than it was, downcast, puffed up, shrinking, frightened? And what will you find which is sufficient reason for this?
8.46: Nothing can happen to any man which is not a human accident, nor to an ox which is not according to the nature of an ox, nor to a vine which is not according to the nature of a vine, nor to a stone which is not proper to a stone. If, then, what happens to each thing is both usual and natural, why should you complain? For the common nature brings nothing which you cannot bear.
8.47: If you are pained by any external thing, it is not this thing that disturbs you, but your own judgement about it. And it is in your power to wipe out this judgement now. But if anything in your own disposition gives you pain, who stops you from correcting your opinion? And even if you are pained because you are not doing some particular thing which seems to you to be right, why do you not act rather than complain?—But some insurmountable obstacle is in the way.—Do not be grieved, then, for the cause of its not being done does not depend on you.—But it is not worth living if this cannot be done.—Then leave life contentedly, just as a man dies who is in full activity, and well pleased, too, with the things that are obstacles.
8.48: Remember that the ruling faculty is invincible when, collected in itself, it is satisfied with itself, if it does nothing which it does not choose to do, even if it resists out of mere stubbornness. What, then, will it be when it forms a judgement about anything with the help of reason and deliberately? Therefore the mind which is free from passions is a citadel, for man has nothing more secure in which he can take refuge and be impregnable from then on. He, then, who has not seen this is an ignorant man; but he who has seen it and does not take refuge here is unhappy.
8.49: Say nothing more to yourself than what the first appearances report. Suppose that it has been reported to you that a certain person speaks ill of you. This has been reported; but that you have been harmed, that has not been reported. I see that my child is sick. I do see it; but that he is in danger, I do not see. So always keep to the first appearances, and add nothing yourself from within, and then nothing happens to you. Or rather, add something, like a man who knows everything that happens in the world.
8.50: A cucumber is bitter.—Throw it away.—There are briars in the road.—Turn aside from them.—This is enough. Do not add, And why were such things made in the world? For you will be laughed at by a man who understands nature, just as you would be laughed at by a carpenter and a shoemaker if you found fault because you see shavings and cuttings in their workshop from the things they make. And yet they have places into which they can throw these shavings and cuttings, and the universal nature has no space outside itself; but the wonderful part of her art is that though she has set limits to herself, everything within her which seems to decay and grow old and be useless she changes into herself, and again makes other new things from these very same, so that she needs neither substance from outside nor a place into which she may throw what decays. She is content, then, with her own space, and her own matter, and her own craft.
8.51:
Do not be sluggish in your actions, nor rambling in your conversation, nor wandering in your thoughts; do not let there be inner conflict in your soul, nor outward outbursts; nor in life be so busy as to have no leisure.

Suppose that men kill you, cut you in pieces, curse you. What can these things do to prevent your mind from remaining pure, wise, sober, just? For instance, if a man should stand by a clear, pure spring and curse it, the spring never stops sending up drinkable water; and if he should throw clay or filth into it, it will quickly disperse them and wash them out, and will not be polluted at all. How, then, will you have a never-failing fountain, and not a mere well? By shaping yourself every hour towards freedom joined with contentment, simplicity, and modesty.
8.52: He who does not know what the world is does not know where he is. And he who does not know for what purpose the world exists does not know who he is, nor what the world is. But he who has failed in any one of these things could not even say for what purpose he himself exists. What, then, do you think of him who avoids or seeks the praise of those who applaud, of men who know neither where they are nor who they are?
8.53: Do you wish to be praised by a man who curses himself three times every hour? Would you wish to please a man who does not please himself? Does a man please himself who regrets nearly everything that he does?
8.54: No longer let your breathing alone act in concert with the air which surrounds you, but let your intelligence also now be in harmony with the intelligence which embraces all things. For the intelligent power is no less spread through all parts and pervading all things for him who is willing to draw it to himself than the power of the air for him who is able to breathe it.
8.55: In general, wickedness does no harm at all to the universe; and in particular the wickedness of one man does no harm to another. It is harmful only to him who has it in his power to be released from it as soon as he chooses.
8.56: To my own free will the free will of my neighbour is just as indifferent as his poor breath and flesh. For though we are made especially for the sake of one another, still the ruling power of each of us has its own office; otherwise my neighbour's wickedness would be my harm, which God has not willed, so that my unhappiness may not depend on another.
8.57: The sun seems to be poured down, and indeed it is spread in all directions, yet it is not poured out. For this spreading is extension: so its rays are called Extensions because they are extended. And one may judge what kind of thing a ray is if he looks at the sun's light passing through a narrow opening into a darkened room, for it is extended in a straight line, and is, as it were, divided when it meets any solid body which stands in the way and cuts off the air beyond; but there the light stays fixed and does not slide or fall off. Such, then, ought to be the pouring out and spreading of the understanding: it should in no way be a pouring away, but an extension, and it should make no violent or headlong collision with the obstacles in its way; nor yet fall down, but be fixed, and light up what receives it. For a body will deprive itself of the light if it does not let it in.
8.58: He who fears death fears either the loss of sensation or a different kind of sensation. But if you have no sensation, neither will you feel any harm; and if you acquire another kind of sensation, you will be a different kind of living being and you will not cease to live.
8.59: Men exist for the sake of one another. Teach them, then, or bear with them.
8.60: An arrow moves in one way, the mind in another. The mind indeed, both when it is being cautious and when it is busy with inquiry, moves straight onward none the less, and towards its object.
8.61: Enter into every man's ruling faculty; and also let every other man enter into yours.
